A synonym for a stored procedure
A single row returned by a query
A type of index
questions.explain: Everything between one GO and the next (or the start/end of a script) is one batch.

options: No — it's a signal recognized by client tools like SSMS, not something the SQL Server engine itself sees
Yes, it's a core T-SQL statement

questions.explain: The client tool strips GO out and sends each batch to the server separately — the engine never sees the word GO.

questions.q: Why does a variable declared before GO become unusable after it?
options: A variable only lives for the batch that declared it, and GO starts a new, separate batch
GO deletes all variables in the entire session
Variables are never allowed before a GO statement
This is actually not true — variables survive GO just fine
questions.explain: This is the practical, common gotcha that trips up developers who don't understand batch boundaries.

questions.q: What does the GO right after USE accomplish at the top of this course's scripts?
options: Ensures the database-context switch completes as its own batch before anything else runs
It has no real purpose and is purely decorative
It deletes the previous database context
It is required syntax for USE to work at all
questions.explain: This ties back to Lesson 2 — some statements must be the first in their batch, so isolating USE this way is a safety habit.

questions.q: What is the fix for a script that errors because a variable was declared before a GO and used after it?
options: Remove the GO between the DECLARE and the usage, keeping them in the same batch
Add another DECLARE statement after GO with the exact same name and no value
Replace GO with a semicolon
This cannot be fixed — variables can never be used across multiple statements
questions.explain: Keeping the declaration and usage in the same batch (no GO between them) resolves the issue.
